newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Versatile Tsui said right for top HK exchange job.
newsitem.headline: Versatile Tsui said right for top HK exchange job.

text.p: Alec Tsui Yui Wa is the right man for the job as chief executive of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong, former colleagues said on Thursday.
"He had a good reputation at the SFC," said a former colleague at the Securities and Futures Commission. "He was designated for a top spot here."
The SFC formally approved Tsui as the exchange's new chief executive on Thursday. Now deputy chief executive, Tsui will take over from Paul Chow on February 1, 1997.
Former colleagues and friends said Tsui is an innovative thinker capable of sharing his long-term plans with his team.
They said he is decisive, sincere, quick to grasp problems and a good team player.
"His strengths are that he is a good all-rounder, quick to learn, and has good interpersonal relationships at all levels," said a former colleague.
Hong Kong-born Tsui, 47, has had a varied career and has been well-liked and respected by superiors and subordinates.

After completing bachelor and master degrees in industrial engineering in the United States, Tsui returned to Hong Kong to work as a systems consultant at Arthur Andersen & Co and then at Swire Bottlers Ltd.
Beginning in 1980, he spent eight years at China Light and Power where he developed abilities in systems management, finance, and corporate planning and management.
In late 1988, Tsui was hired by the then provisional SFC and worked closely with former chairman Robert Owen on the official establishment of the commission in May 1989.

Tsui's first responsibilities at the SFC were similar to his work at China Light & Power, focusing on the set-up of computer-based systems for financial planning and corporate planning and management.
Tsui joined the stock exchange in 1994 as an executive director in charge of finance and operations services. In January 1996, he was appointed deputy chief executive.
"He keeps a low profile but he has a game plan," said another former colleague, adding that Tsui has the ability and willingness to share his long-term plans with subordinates.
While Tsui has said he will hold a steady course at the exchange, friends said they expected him to make his mark.
"He is good at strategic thinking. I can't say he is good at details but he is certainly innovative and he will do something innovative at the exchange," one friend said.
Other ex-colleagues said Tsui thrives on challenges but was not a political person.
"The job of chief executive is a balancing act," said C.C. Goh, managing director of Sassoon Securities in Hong Kong.
"The Hong Kong exchange has 500 member firms with capitalisations ranging from HK$500,000 to HK$500 million," Goh said. "Members' interests are very different."
